<reason>Side B wins on the central distinction: a higher headline price is visible for today's comparison, while a shrunken familiar pack falsely signals continuity. B also shows the notice bans nothing, preserves price points, and supplies current unit price, then weighs certain invisibility against possible misreading. Side A's steering and skimpflation risks are real, but its memory argument conflates detecting a past rise with comparing prices now present, and B plausibly answers that reformulation is neither free nor created by this duty.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Most decisive was B's Rebuttal 2: shoppers need no memory to see £2.00 beside £2.50 today, but cannot see that the £2.00 pack fell to 180g; even if A's tiny-print concern remains, partial visibility beats guaranteed concealment.</best_rebuttal>
